DESCRIPTION: Where the books in Source Library say a person feels alive, the world is alive, or a made thing is alive: {{points}} confirmed passages from {{books}} books, each linked to its page.
DRAFTFLAG: Working draft, 13 October 2026. Every passage on this page was found by a phrase or a probe sentence, read by one model and confirmed by a second, and the second pass was checked by a third reader on a blind sample of {{second_rater.n}} passages (agreement {{second_rater.agree}} of {{second_rater.n}}, Cohen’s kappa {{second_rater.kappa}}). No human scholar has checked it yet. Every quotation is word for word from Source Library’s English translation, and every mark links to its page, so each one can be checked against the scan.
INTRO:
“Aliveness” means at least three different things, and this library holds all three. A person can feel alive, or feel dead inside. The world, or some part of it, can be said to be alive: a soul in the cosmos, seed in metals, souls that move the stars. And a made thing can be said to be alive: a statue a rite has filled with a god, a figure so lifelike it seems about to speak, the quality Christopher Alexander called life in buildings and towns.

This page maps where the books in Source Library say each of these, using the method of the map of conscious experiences, and says how often they say it. The three senses are kept apart as three lanes on one map, because the interesting question is where they meet. Mostly, they do not.
FINDINGS:
What the books say

1. The books put life in the world, not in the person

Of {{points}} confirmed passages, {{confirmed.world_alive}} say that the world or some part of it is alive. Only {{confirmed.felt_alive}} describe, from the inside, what it is like to feel alive, and {{confirmed.felt_dead}} what it is like to feel dead inside. The probes for felt aliveness retrieved {{felt_probes.retrieved}} passages; of the {{felt_probes.judged}} the screen passed to the judge, {{felt_probes.confirmed_own}} were confirmed. They found joy, grief, rapture and relief in quantity, but rarely described as being alive. On a blind random draw of {{baseline_n}} corpus pages, {{baseline_any.confirmed}} touch any layer ({{baseline_any.rate.0}}%, 95% interval {{baseline_any.rate.1}}–{{baseline_any.rate.2}}%), all of them on the world or made-thing layers, and none describes felt aliveness.

The felt passages that do exist are vivid. Swedenborg: “Consequently, all the perceptive and sensitive faculties seemed alive with happiness.” Petrarch on his melancholy: “…a time not of light or life, but resembles a Tartarean night.”

2. What is alive: the cosmos, metals, the heavens

In the world layer the classifier names what is said to be alive: the cosmos as a whole ({{world_carriers.0.1}} passages), metals and minerals ({{world_carriers.1.1}}), the heavens and stars ({{world_carriers.2.1}}), the earth ({{world_carriers.3.1}}), plants ({{world_carriers.4.1}}). The life most often comes from a soul or form ({{world_sources.0.1}}), then from seed and growth ({{world_sources.1.1}}), then from God ({{world_sources.2.1}}) and from a breath or spirit ({{world_sources.3.1}}). Ficino, translating Plato: “it must be said that this world is an animal, truly constituted by divine providence.” The Theatrum chemicum: “Since, therefore, metals grow and have a beginning, it also follows that they are multiplied.”

3. Living matter peaks in the 1600s, the same century dead matter arrives

Counted by phrase alone, with no model involved: the vocabulary of growing metals runs at {{lexical.dims.living_minerals.rate.0}} occurrences per 10,000 translated pages in editions before 1400, {{lexical.dims.living_minerals.rate.3}} in the 1600s and {{lexical.dims.living_minerals.rate.5}} in the 1800s. The soul of the world peaks in the 1600s at {{lexical.dims.world_soul.rate.3}} and falls to {{lexical.dims.world_soul.rate.5}}. The vocabulary of dead matter (“brute matter”, “inert matter”, “automata”) stands at {{lexical.dims.dead_matter.rate.1}} in the 1400s, rises to {{lexical.dims.dead_matter.rate.3}} in the 1600s and stays near that level. Henry More, 1662: “Matter is inert, or destitute of vital sympathy and shared activity”. The argument also ran inside alchemy: Michael Maier, 1618, “In metals, no nutrition, growth, or extension in all dimensions is found”. These counts describe the editions this library holds, dated by the edition, not European thought at large.

4. Made things live by craft or by rite, and buildings do not live at all

{{confirmed.made_alive}} passages call a made thing alive. Most are images and statues ({{made_carriers.0.1}}) and other crafted works ({{made_carriers.1.1}}); the life comes from the maker’s skill ({{made_sources.0.1}}) or from a consecration ({{made_sources.1.1}}). The Hermetic Asclepius supplies the most repeated sentence, in edition after edition, Augustine’s City of God among them: “I mean animated statues, full of sense and spirit, performing such great and such kinds of things.” Life given by a rite can also leave: Gaffarel’s talisman, after its hour, “remains void and useless, cold and dead.” Alexander’s sense, the life of a place, a garden or a building, has almost no counterpart here: the probes for living places, gardens, buildings as bodies, wholeness and the spirit of a place retrieved {{alexander.retrieved}} passages and {{alexander.confirmed}} were confirmed. In these passages a temple can be proportioned like a human body without being called alive.

5. The three senses live in different books

Of the {{books}} books with a confirmed passage, {{books_by_layers.1}} contribute to one layer only and {{books_by_layers.2}} to two; none to all three. The table below sets this out, with the caution it needs.

6. Phrases find this material; embeddings mostly do not

Searching the translations for the phrases translators use (“soul of the world”, “seed of metals”, “animated statues”) confirmed {{lanes.lexical.confirm_of_judged.0}}% of the passages the judge read. Searching by meaning, with probe sentences in the embedding space, confirmed {{lanes.embedding.confirm_of_judged.0}}% (n={{lanes.embedding.judged}}, judging still under way), close to what a random page gives. The same thing limited the map of conscious experiences: the embedding space is organised by book and language more than by idea.
LEX_INTRO: Before any model reads anything, the phrases themselves can be counted. Each panel is one dimension’s set of phrases, counted across every translated page in the library and divided by the number of translated pages in that century’s editions. Green is the world, pink made things, blue the person; the dashed line is dead matter.
RATES_INTRO: The random columns give the base rate: {{baseline_n}} pages drawn blind from the whole translated corpus in July 2026, read again here by the same two passes. The first pass, a fast model, flagged {{baseline_any.screened}} of them ({{baseline_any.screen_rate.0}}%), which is why it is only a screen; the second pass kept {{baseline_any.confirmed}}. The last column counts confirmed passages among the retrieved ones, which depend on how many probes each layer had and so are comparable only within a row.
QUAL_INTRO: The first pass also tagged which qualities a passage gives to the life it describes, from a fixed list of twenty that includes Alexander’s terms (wholeness, proportion, belonging, interiority). Each bar is the share of confirmed passages naming that quality.
MEET_INTRO: Each row asks: among books with one kind of passage, how many also have another kind? A book enters this sample through the one or two passages a probe happened to find, so “without” means “not found here”, not “absent from the book”. The pattern is still strong: the books that call the world alive almost never turn up a passage of felt aliveness.
METHOD:
1. Probes. 25 dimensions in three layers, each with an opposite (feeling dead inside, matter as mechanism, lifeless work). Two lanes: four first-person or period-voice probe sentences per dimension searched over 4.54 million page embeddings, language-stratified; and 151 English phrases searched as exact phrases over the English translations (133 hit; the zero-hit ones are listed in the data).
  2. Screen. gemini-3.1-flash-lite marks each passage on each layer, and must quote, word for word, the sentence that shows it. A layer whose quotation is not on the page is discarded. The comparison ignores inline notes and markup but not words.
  3. Judge. Every screened positive is re-read by gemini-3.8-flash on a strict rubric: a layer stands only if a careful reader would agree the passage states it outright. Analogies, allegory, plain emotion words and ordinary biology are rejected; reported doctrines (“Plato holds the world is an animal”) count.
  4. Second reader. Claude (Opus), a different model family, read {{second_rater.n}} lexical-lane passages blind to the judge: 20 the judge confirmed, 20 it rejected, 20 the screen passed over. It agreed with all 20 confirmations, would have accepted 4 of the 20 rejections, and 6 of the 20 screen negatives. Those 6 exposed the strict quotation check discarding true quotations over markup; the check was fixed and the 550 affected passages screened again. Rates on this page are therefore a floor.
  5. Base rate. The {{baseline_n}}-page blind random sample from the July map, read by the same two passes.

Classification is by models, in English translation. A passage the translation softened or a model misread can be missing; a passage on the map can be wrong. Each one links to its page so it can be checked.
DATA_NOTE: Every point on the map, with its quotation, book, date, language, layer, judge’s reason and page link, is in aliveness-data.json; every figure on this page is in aliveness-numbers.json. The pipeline is in the Source Library repository under scripts/analysis/experience-map/ (probes-aliveness.json, retrieve-aliveness-lexical.mjs, classify-aliveness.mjs, judge-aliveness.mjs, build-aliveness.py). The model reading cost about $8; the counts cost nothing.
